summary:
Analog is an interactive world map and a 3D globe interface that helps researchers find places on Earth that resemble a chosen site on the Moon or Mars and vise versa. Today, analog fieldwork concentrates on a few famous sites, and the field’s own reviews note that there are no standard criteria for choosing them and that valuable sites go overlooked.
We put Earth, the Moon, and Mars on one common grid of about 55 km cells and measured them the same way, using open data from NASA and other agencies: elevation from lunar and Martian orbiters, plus land cover, biomass and climate for Earth. Cells that clearly don’t qualify (forest, cities, open water) are optionally filtered out, and the rest are ranked by how closely their terrain matches the target with adjustable weights. A researcher picks a target and an activity and gets a ranked shortlist of regions, including ones outside the usual list.
It is a screening tool: it compares terrain statistics, not rock type or fine detail, and Earth cannot reproduce low gravity or vacuum. Next steps are surface material and temperature for all three bodies, and finer resolution on the best matches alongside custom experiment settings.
details:
Analoge is an interactive world map for NASA Space Apps 2026 (Edmonton). It helps aerospace start-ups and researchers with limited resources find places on Earth that resemble the surface of the Moon or Mars for a specific activity. The user picks a target body, then one or more activities: spacewalk (EVA), rover testing, craters, or cave exploration. They can also narrow the results by average temperature and elevation. The map then shows only the 0.5° cells that meet every filter, coloured by body (amber for Moon, rust for Mars, purple for both) and brighter where the quality score is higher. Clicking a cell opens a detail card with its coordinates, temperature, elevation, and per-activity label, quality and Moon/Mars scores. 

How it works

  • Data: the analysis produces a single file of about 95,000 land cells on a 0.5° grid. For each activity, a cell has a label (not a site, Moon, Mars or both), a quality score, and separate Moon and Mars scores. The file also carries temperature and elevation per cell. It is loaded once in the browser, so there is no server.
  • Filtering: the data is converted to typed arrays on load. Each filter change re-checks all cells in one pass: any selected target matches, all selected activities must match, and temperature and elevation must fall in range. Because it is client-side, results update instantly.
  • Drawing: matching cells are painted onto an offscreen canvas aligned to the web-mercator map, with opacity set by quality. The canvas is passed to MapLibre as an image layer, over a faint layer of all land cells so context is never lost. When several activities are selected, the colour uses the combined label and the brightness uses the lowest quality among them.
  • Interface: a collapsible sidebar (a bottom sheet on mobile), a detail card, a legend with a live match counter, and an “About the data” window that marks which layers are real and which are demo data. Controls are keyboard-accessible, and body labels appear as text as well as colour.

Benefits

  • It turns a large analysis into something a person can explore in seconds, without GIS software and the ability to more easily incorporate new data.
  • It shows where several needs overlap, for example, a Mars-like site that also works for rover testing and cave exploration, which a single map layer can’t.
  • It makes quality visible, so the best candidates stand out and can be ranked.
  • Being honest about data helps credibility: demo layers are clearly badged.
  • It runs from static files, so it is easy to host and share.

Goals

Analog sites are usually chosen because someone on the team already knows the place. We wanted to replace that with a search of the whole planet that a small team could run without GIS expertise or a data budget. We wanted the users to start from their own expertise on what is valid for their test or draw from known and adjustable data such as Mars rover tests,  moon walks, cave surveys, and more. Using our tool they’d get back places described by numbers they can compare and understand in more depth than desert and mountain. We also wanted to compare terrain directly across three worlds, so that a user can pick a real destination such as Shackleton rim or Jezero crater and see where on Earth is most like it for further investigation and specific analysis.

What we set out to do:

  • Find Earth analogs for the Moon and Mars from open data, as the challenge asks, and describe each one with numbers and reasons rather than a name on a list.
  • Let the user start from what they need to test (a rover, a suit, a cave survey) rather than from a location.
  • Compare terrain directly across three worlds, so a user can pick a real destination such as Shackleton rim or Jezero crater and see where on Earth is most like it.
  • Keep every decision inspectable. A cell that is ruled out says which rule removed it, and any layer that is not yet real data is labelled as demo data.

What comes next:

  • Replace the demo layers (rover testing, spacewalk, craters, elevation) with real data: ASTER emissivity for sand, ETOPO elevation, and impact-crater databases.
  • Back the Moon and Mars target profiles with measured values and sources, in place of our reasoned estimates.
  • Check the rankings against field sites that agencies already use, beyond the handful we tested.
  • Work at a finer grid than 55 km, so small sites are not hidden by their surroundings.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS (and Python for preparing and checking the data).
  • Frameworks and libraries: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand for state, MapLibre GL JS for the map, and Lucide for icons.
  • Map tiles: OpenStreetMap (no key needed), styled dark in the browser for one visual. We use Esri world imagery and Nasa Solar System Treks imager (LRO WAC mosaic for the moon and Viking MDIM 2.1 for mars)
  • Data: a columnar JSON file of 95,447 cells.
  • Environment: Node.js and npm, running in the browser. Testing used a headless Chromium browser.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on an ordinary laptop or phone with a modern browser and a graphics-capable browser (WebGL).

AI was used to help us understand the data, create code, documentation and presentation for this project.
